speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY   EXCHANGE OF LETTERS BETWEEN SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS AND UNITED STATES AMBASSADOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to table an exchange of two letters in English and in French between myself and the United States ambassador to Canada concerning the St. Lawrence seaway project. This exchange embodies certain conclusions reached as a result of the recent discussions between representatives of the two governments.
The two main conclusions are: First, the United States administration will seek approval of congress to be relieved of the necessity under public law 358 of duplicating the canal which the Canadian government proposes to build at Iroquois. Secondly, the Canadian government states that it does not propose under present conditions to duplicate the navigation facilities for 27 feet or lesser draft on opposite sides of the St. Lawrence river to by-pass the dams in the Cornwall-Barnhart island area.
In short, Mr. Speaker, it is the intention of both governments not to duplicate under present conditions navigation work under construction which by-passes the international rapids section.

1.	In recent years has there been any improvement in the mental health situation in Canada?
2.	Has there been any increase in government expenditures on mental health in recent years?

1. Yes. The program against mental illness in Canada is showing heartening results which gives grounds for anticipating increased future improvement. Some of the statistics are indicative of this trend. For instance the time required to treat certain illnesses in Canadian mental hospitals has decreased. For patients of all diagnoses discharged from these hospitals in 1948 the average duration of treatment was 18 months. By 1953 the period of treatment required for all diagnoses was reduced to just under 10 months. For schizophrenia, which constitutes one of the largest single groups of mental illness, the average stay in hospital was 24 months in 1948; this was decreased by 1953 to an average of just under 14 months.
The federal mental health grant has had a major impact on the mental health program of Canada. There has been a very sharp increase in the number of treating personnel available to the mental health field and a very rapid extension of the services available for the treatment and prevention of mental illness.

Orders for Returns
Our improved health education program is bringing more people to hospital for earlier treatment. The emphasis on prevention of serious mental illness and its increasing acceptance by the general public is a most encouraging sign. Attitudes towards mental illness are changing for the better and the public have come to know that Canadian mental hospitals compare most favourably with similar facilities in the United States and other countries. Indicative of this trend is the fact that 20 per cent of all new admissions in 1953 were voluntary, whereas in 1943 this figure was only 5 per cent. It is impossible to measure the benefits of the mental health movement which has permeated all strata of Canadian society today.
2. Yes. The awareness that this improvement can only be maintained through increasing expenditures is shown by the willingness of all levels of government to provide for mental health expenditures. There has been a threefold increase in the ten-year period from 1943 to 1953 in so far as Canadian mental hospitals are concerned. Operating costs for mental health hospitals in 1953-54 were $5 million more than in the previous year. Community mental health clinics, too, represent a tremendous investment in the preventive mental health program, increasing as they have in the past five years from 17 to more than 100.

For a copy of all correspondence exchanged between the minister or Department of Transport and the Canadian National Railways relative to a question placed on the order paper in the name of the mover of this matter on the 28th January last, the purpose of which was to ascertain the number of section and maintenance men, office staffs, etc., who have been laid off by the Canadian National Railways during the periods particularly set forth in the said question.

Mr. Speaker, by this motion the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) asks that the house order the production of all correspondence between the minister or the Department of Transport and the Canadian National Railways relative to a question which the hon. member placed on the order paper on January 28 last, the purpose of which was to ascertain the number of section and maintenance men, office staffs, etc., who have been laid off by the Canadian National Railways during certain periods. 1 can only repeat what I said a few days ago upon another motion introduced by the same hon. member, namely that correspondence between the minister or officials of the Department of Transport and the Canadian National Railways is privileged and has always been so regarded I think by this house. For that reason I think that an order for its production ought not to be voted by the house.

Mr. Speaker, may I rise on a point of order affecting the privileges of the house. In answer to my hon. friend I would point out that this is not an endeavour to secure information with regard to internal management or correspondence of an interdepartmental character. When the question was asked the minister took the stand that the information was not readily procurable when he answered on February 21 and stated as follows, as reported at page 1326 of Hansard:
This is another question which cannot be answered completely without the assignment of a special staff. Here again, the information would have to be assembled at the 42 divisions of the company, and would then have to be consolidated.
I point out, sir, that what I am trying to do is to ascertain not a matter of internal management because the minister has no jurisdiction in any way over the railway except to report to parliament. At least that

Motions for Papers
is the contention he has made in the past. What I am trying to find out is whether the minister has properly placed the matter before the railway company so that information which it would not be difficult to ascertain could be ascertained, namely the number of lay-offs on the Canadian National Railways. I am trying to find out whether the matter has in fact been placed before the company and whether the company is refusing to give information which parliament has a right to ask.

Mr. Speaker, may I say quite frankly that I thought the motion had some such implication as my hon. friend suggests; but it seems to me that when I answered the question orally the other day I told him that I was giving the information which I had obtained from the Canadian National Railways and I observe that in effect this motion asks for the production of the correspondence which I exchanged with the president of the Canadian National Railways in order to obtain the answer to my hon. friend's question. The purpose of this motion seems to be to verify whether the answer I gave to the house is in conformity with the information I obtained from the president of the railway. I may say that I was somewhat unwilling to think that was the intention of the hon. member but what he has said leads me to believe that my inference was correct. However, I do not raise that question in objecting to the motion. I think that the correspondence between the minister and the president of the Canadian National Railways is privileged. It has been so held in the past by this house, and I invoke that fact as an argument against the adoption of the motion.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I would place before you and before the house the thought that this correspondence referred to by the minister relates to information sought by the house. It is therefore a matter in which the House of Commons, I submit, has a definite interest. As the hon. member for Prince Albert pointed out, the purpose of this motion is not to seek details of the internal management but to seek details as to the correspondence which passed between the minister and the president of the railway with regard to information requested by a member of this House of Commons. As such I submit that it is perfectly within the rights of this house to require production of that correspondence because it is correspondence concerning matters raised in the House of Commons itself.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, may I ask a question or make a suggestion? A few days ago, in answering
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
the question referred to and similar questions of mine, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) said that he was prepared to try to get such information as was available that might meet the questions we were asking at least in part. I wonder whether this matter could not be left standing until the minister has given us that information?
Mr. Speaker, ordinarily I would have no objection, but I am trying to get through that curtain of secrecy and I think the matter should be disposed of.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member has made the matter a question of order. I might say that there are two points at issue. One is one which is of a general character which is being invoked not only when there are motions for the production of papers relating to C.N.R. management or C.N.R. affairs but whenever it concerns correspondence between the minister and his officials, whether they be officials of the C.N.R. or officials of his own department. That, I think, will be agreed upon by the house as being an attitude which has always been taken by ministers and recognized as being the only one they can take. Bourinot, fourth edition, at page 251 says:
The practice of asking for reports from officers, addressed to particular departments of the executive government, is considered to be open to serious objection.
That has been the practice of ministers in the house ever since there has been an executive. On that particular point I do not think the hon. member can insist. What he has asked for is a copy of all correspondence exchanged between the minister or Department of Transport and the Canadian National Railways respecting certain affairs. Maybe the minister, in order to get his information, did not write anything. Maybe he just telephoned. Whatever exchange took place between the minister and some other person with respect to this particular matter is, as the minister has said, privileged. If there are any documents, they are privileged documents and they are not to be asked for in the house. That has been the practice followed and accepted by the house.
The other point has reference to the last remark of the hon. member who wants to peek through the curtain of secrecy, as he calls it. That is a debatable point between the opposition and the government as to whether the present government should follow, with respect to C.N.R. affairs and information pertaining to them, the same attitude followed in the past by other governments occupying the treasury benches. The only way I can deal with the matter from the point of view of order is to inform the hon, member that the practice of governments

since 1921 of giving this type of reply to similar questions or notices of motions for production of papers placed on the order paper has had an effect on the Chair. The effect it has had has been rather extreme in certain cases, and I will only quote one ruling given in the session of 1932-33 which is to be found at page 694 of Hansard of October 31, 1932. Mr. Desrochers moved a motion for production of papers in the following terms:
For a copy of all documents, letters and protests, in the possession of the Canadian National Railways with respect to mile post 35, Quebec-Chicoutimi division since 1917.
Mr. Speaker said:
The government have declined to supply similar information, on the ground that it is entirely for the railway company, therefore this resolution is out of order.
I could quote several rulings by my predecessors to the same effect. I wish that hon. members might find a way of further arguing, if they so wish, whether the policy followed by the government with respect to these matters is the right one. I suggest that perhaps Mr. King did in 1921 when he moved an amendment to the motion to go into supply. In that debate he said that it was the undoubted right of parliament to have all this information pertaining to the C.N.R. Mr. King's amendment is to be found at page 1178 of Hansard of March 22, 1921, and is in these words:
Subject to the reservation that in exceptional cases there may be documents of a confidential character which, in the public interest, may properly be withheld from publication, the house declares that it is the undoubted right of parliament to demand and receive copies of all reports, accounts, correspondence and papers in relation to the management of every department of the public service including the affairs of the Canadian National Railways, whether operating directly under the control of the department or under corporate form.
A debate ensued, and Mr. Meighen's position is to be found at page 1180. What came out of this debate was the establishment of a committee, a practice which has been followed ever since. Mr. King suggested at page 1180 that there were three methods by which information pertaining to the C.N.R. could be supplied to the house. He said:
It is customary in this house to have information given in answer to questions addressed to the ministry, or on motions for the production of papers; and sometimes the information is given through special committees.
Before the debate on the amendment to the motion to go into supply terminated, there was a motion by the government for the creation of a committee on railways and shipping. Hon. members will find the order of reference of the first committee established to examine the affairs of the C.N.R. at page
Motions for Papers
164 of the Journals of 1921, volume 58. I quote:
And the question being put on the main motion as amended, as follows:
That a select standing committee on national railways and shipping be appointed for the present session, and be instructed to inquire into the following question:
1.	What information as to operations of Canadian National Railways and shipping as conducted by the board of directors and management should, in the public interest, be brought down in parliament on question, motion for production of papers, or otherwise,
2.	When, by what method, and under what conditions, if any, should such information be given, regard being had for the necessity of securing to parliament and the public all facts requisite for the determination of policy, including finance, and to the board of directors the best possible conditions for efficiency of management,
3.	What system of auditing should be adopted, and what extent of detail should be given in the annual report,
4.	What if any improvement could be made in the general scheme of management,
5.	Whether and for what purposes the said committee should be continued, and that for the above purposes and for such other purposes as the committee deem in the public interest there be referred to said committee the annual report of the board of directors and that the said committee have power to examine witnesses under oath, to send for papers, persons, and records and to report from time to time.
This committee was the father of all the committees on railways and government-owned shipping since that time. As I said, I deal with these matters merely because, as I have indicated, the practice adopted on this very question in 1921 after several debates has resulted in Mr. Speaker of the day and his successors intervening in the fashion which I have indicated to say that the matter is not in order and to remove a motion for production of papers completely from the order paper without even giving a chance for members to ask for a protest vote.
As I say, it is a debatable point whether the practice of answering questions pertaining to C.N.R. affairs should be continued by way of a committee or otherwise. I am not going to say anything about that, but as far as the merit of the answer given today by the minister is concerned, 1 will have to decide that such an answer has been found proper on similar occasions in respect of all such matters, and therefore I cannot rule in the manner which the hon. member for Prince Albert would like me to do at this moment. The motion is dropped.

subtopic: REPORTED OBJECTION TO USE OP WORD "ROYAL" IN NAME OF TRANSCONTINENTAL TRAIN

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REPORTED OBJECTION TO USE OP WORD "ROYAL" IN NAME OF TRANSCONTINENTAL TRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday last the Leader of the Opposition asked me if I had
1552	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry any comments to make to the house in regard to the positive statement in Sunday's edition of the New York Times that the Canadian Pacific Railway planned to call its new transcontinental train the "Royal Canadian", but that the government objected to this and as a result part of the name, "Royal", has been dropped. I do not wish to make any comments but merely to state the facts, which are quite simple.
Prior to the publication of this statement, no member of the government had heard anything at all about the plans to call a C.P.R. train the "Royal Canadian". When I made inquiries last week in that regard I was informed that what had happened was this. The under-secretary of state noticed an item in the newspapers sometime last December about a new transcontinental passenger train which the Canadian Pacific proposed to put into service under the name the "Royal Canadian". As there had been no communication with the department about this he wrote to Mr. N. R. Crump, vicepresident of the Canadian Pacific, on December 31 last inquiring as to whether the Canadian Pacific had obtained permission to use that name. A few days later he was informed by telephone that the general solicitor of the Canadian Pacific would come to see him at an early date to discuss this question with him. The general solicitor did come to see him and contended that no permission was required to use that name. The under-secretary expressed the view that it could not be used without permission and they discussed the proper interpretation of section 9 of the Trade Marks Act. The language of that section is, in part, as follows:
(1) No person shall adopt In connection with a business, as a trade mark or otherwise, any mark consisting of, or so nearly resembling as to be likely to be mistaken for
(d) any word or symbol likely to lead to the belief that the wares or services in association with which it is used have received or are produced, sold or performed under royal, vice-regal or governmental patronage, approval or authority.
Subsection 2 provides:
Nothing in this section prevents the use as a trade mark or otherwise, in connection with a business, of any mark described in subsection (1) with the consent of Her Majesty or such other person, society, authority or organization as may be considered to have been intended to be protected by this section.
The general solicitor maintained his view on the legal aspect of the problem but indicated that it would be for the administrative authorities of the company to decide as a matter of policy what they would do.
On January 20, 1955, the general solicitor wrote to the under-secretary of state that after consideration the management had informed him that because of the time element


for releases and the inability to bring the matter to a conclusion quickly they would abandon the use of the word "royal" in regard to the train and simply call it "The Canadian".

subtopic: REPORTED OBJECTION TO USE OP WORD "ROYAL" IN NAME OF TRANSCONTINENTAL TRAIN
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister if the government has any objection to the use of this name by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company?

subtopic: REPORTED OBJECTION TO USE OP WORD "ROYAL" IN NAME OF TRANSCONTINENTAL TRAIN
speechtext:
The government has no objection, but the government feels that every request for such use should be submitted for the pleasure of Her Majesty, and has taken the position that it does not give constitutional advice but submits the matter for the pleasure of Her Majesty. That has been the practice since the war.
There were quite a few applications during the war for the use of the word "royal" and his late majesty deferred consideration until after the war. There was then a communication addressed to the governor general that of the seven that had been submitted only one would be approved; that it was not likely that the institutions which had been allowed to use the word "royal" would disappear and therefore it was felt at the palace that greater care should be taken to avoid increasing unduly the number of institutions that would be given permission to use the word "royal". There was the comment that the more jealously it was guarded the greater value it would retain.
It is because of that that in many cases the attention of those who wanted to use the word has been called to that attitude and the government does not arrogate to itself any right to say that the word shall not be used. When there is an application it is submitted for Her Majesty's pleasure as being, not only in theory but in fact, the personal prerogative of the sovereign.

subtopic: REPORTED OBJECTION TO USE OP WORD "ROYAL" IN NAME OF TRANSCONTINENTAL TRAIN
speechtext: I take it from the Prime Minister's remarks that it is clear that the government has no objection or will offer no objection to the use of this name by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.

subtopic: REPORTED OBJECTION TO USE OP WORD "ROYAL" IN NAME OF TRANSCONTINENTAL TRAIN
speechtext: The government would offer no objection. I am not trying to defend the attitude of the under-secretary of state, but it was to his knowledge that a little over a year ago another transportation company had said that it wanted to use the name "Royal Canadian" for one of its services. The matter was discussed with those who put it forward. At that time it did not come before the cabinet but the view of the ministers concerned was that it would be unwise to ask for that permission and the matter was dropped.

subtopic: REPORTED OBJECTION TO USE OP WORD "ROYAL" IN NAME OF TRANSCONTINENTAL TRAIN
speechtext: The Prime Minister has not yet made it clear as to what stand the government would take. Will it now object to the use of this word by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company or will it have no objection?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REPORTED OBJECTION TO USE OP WORD "ROYAL" IN NAME OF TRANSCONTINENTAL TRAIN
speechtext:
The matter has never come up for consideration by the government. There never was any request to the government to submit an application from the company to Her Majesty. The only correspondence is made up of the two letters to which I have referred, the last one of which says that as it could not be disposed of quickly the management had decided to abandon the project of securing that name for its train.
This is not something that arises because the government has any objection to the use of the word "royal"; it is because of the attitude that has been taken that it could not be authorized without the permission of the sovereign. I think the language used is that it should be restricted to institutions having as essential qualifications eminence, long standing and secure financial position and devoted to national, charitable or scientific objects. Many organizations throughout the British Empire could justly put forward such claims and in the future they could not be regarded as being in the position where this would be sufficient to justify recognition.
The Trade Marks Act clearly indicates that in the view of parliament this provision was put there for the protection of certain institutions, not because there was any objection to the use of the word. It was felt that it should be protected presumably in the interests of the dignity of the monarchial institution.

subtopic: REPORTED OBJECTION TO USE OP WORD "ROYAL" IN NAME OF TRANSCONTINENTAL TRAIN
speechtext: Apparently some ministers of the crown did consider this question and decided unfavourably. Is the government now willing to consent to the use of this name by the company?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REPORTED OBJECTION TO USE OP WORD "ROYAL" IN NAME OF TRANSCONTINENTAL TRAIN
speechtext: The government has no right to consent to the use of this word.

subtopic: REPORTED OBJECTION TO USE OP WORD "ROYAL" IN NAME OF TRANSCONTINENTAL TRAIN
speechtext: Is the government willing to recommend to the crown that the company be permitted to use it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REPORTED OBJECTION TO USE OP WORD "ROYAL" IN NAME OF TRANSCONTINENTAL TRAIN
speechtext: The position taken by the government is that it makes no recommendation; if it finds that it is something entirely unworthy of consideration by the sovereign it refuses to put it forward. If it finds that it is something that should be considered, as it did find in the case of the Winnipeg ballet, it puts it forward without recommendation but for the pleasure of Her Majesty.

subtopic: REPORTED OBJECTION TO USE OP WORD "ROYAL" IN NAME OF TRANSCONTINENTAL TRAIN

Would the government foe willing to put forward the recommendation without any objection thereto?
Inquiries of the Ministry

subtopic: REPORTED OBJECTION TO USE OP WORD "ROYAL" IN NAME OF TRANSCONTINENTAL TRAIN

subtopic: FORMOSA
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADIAN COMMITMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. What commitments does Canada have toward Formosa arising out of membership in the United Nations?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FORMOSA
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADIAN COMMITMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was good enough to give me notice of his question, which is an important one and somewhat more complicated than it otherwise would be because of the difference of views over the legal status of Formosa. But I am glad to put the viewpoint of the government on record in regard -to this matter, as follows:
As the United Nations has taken no action regarding Formosa we have no commitments to take any action either. Any general obligations arising out of membership in the United Nations would arise only when the United Nations took some action in accordance with the provisions of the charter and called upon members to give assistance or to co-operate.
The question of hostilities in -the area of certain islands off the coast of the mainland of China is on the agenda of the security council. Because of the refusal of the Peking government to send a representative to the security council to discuss this question the council has deferred discussion pending further examination of the problem through diplomatic channels. However, if the security council should decide -to take some action under chapter VI relating to the pacific settlement of disputes, and if it should request

Inquiries of the Ministry any United Nations member government to give assistance by way of good offices or something of that kind, then there would be a moral obligation for us to give that request sympathetic consideration.
There has been no suggestion that the security council should take any action under chapter VII relating to action with respect to threats to the peace, breaches of the peace and acts of aggression, and I would hope that before any suggestion of this kind is made every avenue for peaceful settlement of the disturbed situation in the Formosa strait will be fully explored.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the particular act to be amended by the bill founded on the resolution is one that goes back in the history of our country quite a long time, away back to 1918 in fact. Of course it applies only to persons who come within the service of the federal government. The Government Employees Compensation Act provides for payment of compensation to civil employees of the
[Mr. Green.)

federal government, and to employees of boards, commissions and corporations established to act as agencies of the crown which are brought within the scope of the act by the governor in council, in cases of injury or death sustained in the course of, and arising out of, employment.
At present there are approximately 200,000 employees in these categories who are covered by the act. The legislation is analogous to provincial workmen's compensation legislation which is applicable to employees in private industry and their employers.
The provision for payment of compensation to workers for injury or death sustained in the course of and arising out of the workman's employment is essentially a matter of civil rights and as such falls within the legislative jurisdiction of the provinces. All provinces have enacted workmen's compensation laws. These are not applicable, however, to the crown in right of Canada and its employees.
The purpose of the Government Employees Compensation Act was to afford to employees of the crown a measure of protection similar to that provided to employees of private employers under provincial workmen's compensation laws. Thus the resolution introducing the original government employees' compensation act enacted in 1918 reads as follows:
That an employee in the service of His Majesty who is injured . . . shall be entitled to the same compensation as the employee of a person other than His Majesty would, under similar circumstances, be entitled to receive under the law of the province in which the accident occurs.
The provisions of the present act accordingly provide for this intention. Pursuant to these provisions the provincial workmen's compensation boards have by arrangement handled the adjudication of claims of employees under the federal act as the agent of the federal government.
Our experience with the provincial boards has, I believe, been a mutually satisfactory one. I would like here to express our appreciation of the manner in which our interest and the interests of our employees have been looked after by the provincial workmen's compensation boards. Our injured employees receive good care and are entitled to the same services and facilities as are available to other injured work people. On the very practical matter of costs, I have no reason to depart from the statement I made in this house on May 7, 1952, when I said:
-the objective, of course, in asking the various provincial workmen's compensation boards to act as adjudicators under this act was for the purpose of economy.
Of course, that is still a very important objective. If the provincial governments did

not do this work it would be necessary to set up a fairly ambitious establishment centrally to carry it into effect.
In addition to repaying the boards for all disbursements on claims, the federal government pays to each of the boards a portion of its total administration expenses determined largely by the extent to which we use their services. Here in Ottawa we have a branch in the Department of Labour that looks after general administration and facilitates the handling of the employees' work-injury claims. The branch supplies supplementary information to the boards, checks disbursements, reviews and certifies monthly accounts and, in general, keeps records of all accidents, their cause, the nature of the injuries and so on.
One ordinarily does not regard government service as containing what might be called hazardous occupations. While this may correctly apply to office staffs in general, it should be pointed out that there are many employees doing difficult work of a hazardous nature in research, on surveys, on inspection, in transport, and in remote areas under unusual conditions and circumstances that may involve risks.
For example, the departments presided over by my colleagues, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters), the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) and the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage), as was very much in evidence in the frozen north within the last few days, have employees who are living dangerously.
To illustrate the point, during the fiscal year 1953-54 there were about 15,000 claims; fortunately about two-thirds of these involved "no lost time"-in other words, medical aid only was required. I hardly need mention that in co-operation with other departments efforts are being made towards a reduction in these accidental injuries.
Although the legislation has been amended a few times with respect to particular provisions, there has been no general revision of the act since its inception in 1918. The provisions of the act have been carefully reviewed over the past year and it is considered that a number of the provisions now require amendment and that some new ones should be added in the light of current conditions, needs and practices.
The proposed amendments provide that the entitlement to and rates of compensation payable to an employee under the act shall be determined in accordance with and under the same circumstances as are provided under the law of the province where the employee
Government Employees Compensation Act is usually employed rather than, as at present, under the law of the province where the accident occurred or the industrial disease was contracted.
It is considered that this change will bring the application of the legislation more closely in line with provincial workmen's compensation legislation which applies generally if the employee's usual place of employment is in the province even though the specific accident may have occurred outside the province. It is considered that the change will make for a more equitable and beneficial application of the legislation for employees making claims under the act.
Other proposed amendments will extend the coverage of the act to persons who are not paid a direct wage or salary by the crown but who are otherwise employees; for example, a person on loan to a government agency from private industry.
The amendments will provide for greater uniformity of coverage in the case of employees who are assigned to work outside Canada by providing that for the purposes of the act the usual place of employment of such employees shall be deemed to be Ontario. This means that all claims of such employees will be dealt with by reference to the Ontario workmen's compensation board and the application of the Ontario act.
Changes are also proposed, firstly, in the provisions of the act governing the prosecution of actions instituted by an employee or the crown, under subrogation of the right of the employee, against third parties for damages for negligence in the case of accidents which give rise to claims for compensation under the act; and, secondly, in the provisions governing the disposition of amounts recovered by the crown from third parties in actions of this nature. These changes will operate for the benefit of employees affected.
Under new sections it is proposed that accident prevention activities and safety programs within the federal public service be co-ordinated and further developed. We are also providing that rehabilitation services be clearly stated as among the benefits that are conferred by the legislation.
The bill incorporates in the act a number of other existing compensation measures for special groups and situations which provide some form of compensation either in lieu of or in addition to that provided by the act. It is considered that it would be more satisfactory to have these related measures incorporated in the act. The consolidation of these provisions will, I think, result in better service to our employees and improved administration.

Government Employees Compensation Act
Included also are provisions for compensation to staff locally engaged abroad and additional benefits where an employee dies as a result of an accident while absent on duty from his usual place of employment.
I feel that these proposals will commend themselves to the house, indicative as they are of progress in this field and paralleling in some respects developments that have taken place in the provinces. I shall be very glad to give further detailed explanations as the resolution and bill move forward.

I was intrigued by the minister's comment that government employees were not considered generally to be engaged in hazardous occupations, and then he proceeded to set out various departments in which it was considered there was an element of hazard. I would draw to his attention the fact that even office staffs have accidents on occasion. Indeed I have been somewhat surprised there are not more accidents in the beautiful halls of this very building. Undoubtedly the floors in the halls are beautiful; nevertheless they are very dangerous; and it has always been a surprise to me that more people are not the victims of accidents in those halls and on the marble stairways. However, I suppose those who use this building are now familiar with the danger, and take extra precautions.
Even in the minister's explanation there is a certain degree of vagueness, some of which will be ironed out no doubt when we reach second reading. The first part of the resolution refers to certain persons who are not paid a direct wage. I am wondering however about persons locally engaged outside of Canada-whether it refers to citizens of other countries or only to Canadians who are posted abroad to the various offices of the departments of the Canadian government. Inasmuch as the administration in connection with compensation has always been under the jurisdiction of provincial workmen's compensation boards, I am wondering whether those boards have been consulted and their reactions obtained with regard to this measure.


Then there is the provision for additional benefits where an employee dies as the result of an accident while absent on duty from his usual place of employment. Perhaps when he replies the minister will tell us whether this refers to an increase in death benefits, or refers to expenses incurred by reason of absence from a person's usual place of employment. I would be interested to know, and I am sure other hon. members have a like interest, whether this represents a raising of the rate-although I cannot see how that will be possible, in view of the fact that the provinces have jurisdiction.
The minister referred to the intention to institute some form of accident prevention propaganda, if we may use that word. I have noticed some folders around this building in the last little while, and I am wondering if the sending out of these folders represents a new departure, and whether it is the intention of the Department of Labour to accelerate its activities in this field. In any event, is this program being undertaken in collaboration with the industrial accident prevention society, which works in close conjunction with the workmen's compensation boards of the provinces?
These are thoughts which come to mind, upon hearing the minister's explanation. As I said, when we have the bill before us we will have specific questions to ask with regard to its various clauses. At this stage however it will be interesting to have the minister answer the points I have raised.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with interest to the statement of the Minister of Labour on this resolution, and I think I can say fairly on behalf of members in this group that, speaking generally, we welcome any measure which tends to extend the area of general responsibility covering the hazards of individuals in the course of their employment.
I realize of course that it is impossible to understand fully all that may be involved in the measure until we see the bill-although I think the minister made clear what its general purpose would be. The minister's reference to the extension of this coverage to people employed by the government of Canada outside this country is one of the most interesting features in the legislation. If it does apply-as I am inclined to assume it does, and certainly hope it does-to the nationals of any country who may be engaged from time to time by the government of Canada, this feature in itself should serve to enhance the good name of Canada abroad, wherever the government of this country on behalf of our people may be conducting activities from time to time.

Government Employees Compensation Act
I would be interested to know why the province of Ontario, and its compensation act, has been picked as the province to set the standard for the benefits to be provided in this connection. As I am not a citizen of Ontario, I am not too familiar with the details of the act of this province; nor do I know whether it compares favourably or unfavourably in the rate of benefits with similar provisions in the workmen's compensation act in British Columbia. I notice that this would appear to be an extension of a principle already in the act, where benefits extended to people in the Northwest Territories are tied to the workmen's compensation act of Alberta.
When I read that particular section of the measure I wondered whether that was the soundest principle for the federal government to follow in legislation of this kind. It is my personal opinion that if the federal government in Canada is going to provide coverage to its employees, it could very well have its legislation in such form that the coverage would be at least as good as that provided by any province in Canada. There might be occasions when the legislation in British Columbia would be better than that in Nova Scotia, or the legislation in Nova Scotia better than that in Alberta or Ontario.
It seems to me that the sounder principle, and one that could very well be incorporated in the act, while it is up for review in its application to people outside Canada and others in the northern part of the country to whom it has not applied heretofore would be to see that the federal government would provide coverage as good as that provided anywhere in Canada. Mr. Chairman, as the resolution indicates, this bill will be designed to bring about a minor extension of the benefits under the act, as well as a broadening of the coverage to include certain groups of persons employed in the public service who are not contributors under the act at the present time. In addition there will be a number of amendments dealing with purely administrative points which have arisen during the first year of the operation of this act, which came into force on January 1, 1954.
The new act brought with it the addition of some 60,000 temporary employees as contributors under the act. Nearly all of these persons had periods of prior service for which they might elect to contribute, and it has not proven to be feasible to process the large number of elections made by them within the year provided by the act. Accordingly one of the more important amendments is to permit a limited extension of this election period. I might add that in order to allay concern on this point the Minister of Finance announced last September that it was the government's intention to ask parliament to make this amendment.
The principal extension of coverage proposed under the act would make it possible for the governor in council to designate sessional employees of the Senate and House of Commons as contributors just as is presently done in the case of prevailing rate and seasonal employees.
It turns out that the elections to contribute for prior service are sometimes made on the basis of erroneous information, with the result that when presented with the true cost the contributor may want to back out of the agreement he has made but he is now precluded from doing so by the act. In some cases, perhaps because of illness, the payment of future instalments becomes a financial hardship. One of the proposed amendments will make it possible for a person to revoke 50433-100

He said: Mr. Speaker, I do not know that I have much to add to the statement I made upon introduction and first reading of the bill. In order to explain its principle, may I say that the purpose of the bill is to give legal effect in Canada to the agreement between the government of Canada and the government of Ireland for the avoidance of double taxation and the establishment of rules for reciprocal fiscal assistance in the matter of income taxes.
This agreement was signed at Ottawa on behalf of the government of Canada by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) on the 28th of October, 1954, and was also signed by the ambassador of Ireland. The agreement follows the pattern established in the present income tax agreements which Canada has made with the United States, the United Kingdom, Sweden, New Zealand and France, and has for its purpose the avoidance of double taxation and the exchange of information.
Double taxation is avoided chiefly by a reciprocal system of tax credits in which the country of residence gives credit for the tax imposed by the country where the income has its source. The agreement contains the usual provision limiting the taxation of trading profits to the permanent establishment rule. In addition, certain special provisions are made. Profits from the operation of ships and aircraft will be taxed solely in the country of the residence of the operator.

The bill affects his whole tax, whereas under the agreement we have here which we are asked to approve, only taxes levied by the government of Canada are included. speechtext: Would the hon. member tell us what the point is? We have not heard it down in this part of the chamber.

subtopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND IRELAND FOR THE AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
I have suggested that this agreement with Ireland should include not merely taxes levied by the Dominion of Canada, but that in the case of Ontario there is the question of succession duties. Ontario still levies its own succession duties. Therefore you have a man living in Ontario and another man living in Ireland, which is a unitary state. In Ireland that man's tax will be subject to this agreement. In Ontario the only part of his tax subject to the agreement will be that part which he pays to the dominion which, in the case of succession duties, is much smaller.
I submit that a citizen of Ontario is entitled to have the dominion government act for him in his capacity as a citizen of Ontario as well as that of a dominion taxpayer; for in an agreement which leaves with the province of Ontario the right to levy its own succession duties it is reasonable to suppose that the dominion would get a quid pro quo. In other words I say that the citizen of Ontario is entitled to believe that this agreement should cover the whole of his succession duties. If that is not so, then he is not getting an equal deal vis-a-vis the man who lives in Ireland and who pays a unitary tax.
The minister says to me that this point has been considered. I should say that first of all he seemed just to infer that it had been considered, saying that it must have been. Now he says more positively that it has been considered. He also tells me that one objection to my suggestion is that the dominion cannot negotiate on behalf of the provinces, and that the only agreement the dominion can make is on behalf of itself. However sound that may be in the narrow contemplation of constitutional law, it does not seem to me to make sense; because the province of Ontario cannot itself negotiate an agreement on succession duties with Ireland-at least I assume it cannot. Therefore the only way a citizen of Ontario can have his rights covered is through an agreement made by the federal government on his behalf.
I suggest therefore that this agreement is defective, and that in order to do justice to the citizen of Ontario it should cover not merely succession duties payable to the dominion but payable to Ontario as well; because that is, in essence, the basis of the arrangement made with Ireland, where the Irish citizen is getting a deduction in respect

of his whole tax, not merely a fraction of his tax, which will be the case with the citizen of Ontario.
If I have stated the point correctly, it seems to me it has a measure of common sense in it. Unless the minister can satisfy me that what I have said is unreasonable I should think he would want to be the first to have it withdrawn and looked into further. Not being a man who is in the happy position of always being sure he is right, I have consulted with more than one other person, persons who are competent to have opinions in the matter, and their view is the same as mine; that at any rate this is worth being looked into. For the life of me I cannot understand why the minister should object. If he can satisfy me that I am wrong, I shall have nothing more to say. But if by any chance I should be right, then this should be corrected now.

This is a general definition article. The definition of the term "permanent establishment" in paragraph 1(h) is of particular importance in the application of article III.
Then article III provides that an Irish enterprise will only be taxed in Canada with respect to industrial and commercial profits to the extent that these are attributable to

Income Tax
its permanent establishment in Canada. I might interject a remark at this point with reference to permanent establishment, because this matter has been discussed in connection with former agreements over the years. For instance, it means that if a Canadian manufacturing concern has a place of business, let us say, in Dublin or anywhere else in Ireland and that place is used for display purposes, but the goods which would be sold there would not be actually delivered from that warehouse, then it is not taxable there. But if they have a manufacturing concern in Ireland which makes sales of goods, the profits from that establishment would be taxable. That is what is referred to as a permanent establishment.
The same rule applies reciprocally with respect to the industrial and commercial profits of a Canadian enterprise in Ireland. A subsidiary company is not considered to be a permanent establishment, and the parent company will not be subject to tax in the foreign country on the industrial and commercial profits which its subsidiary earns in that country, except in so far as payments may be made to the parent company by way of dividends, interest, and other similar payments, subject to the further provisions of the agreement.

prevent evasion; second, the granting of credits by the country of domicile for duty paid by the same estate on the same assets to the other contracting country; third, the establishment between the countries of agreed rules of situs. Indeed, this agreement follows the agreement with the United Kingdom, with minor changes, as for example the elimination from the present agreement of possibilities of extension of its terms to colonies.

I shall follow the procedure we followed in connection with the income tax bill. The articles follow as a schedule to the bill.
Article I is a definition of the duties covered by the agreement.
Article II defines the terms "territory" and "duty" and the definition of other terms is agreed upon.
Article III determines the agreed situs of all kinds of property. In the main it follows the British agreement.
Article IV provides for the continuance of deductions allowed by each country, and establishes that rates will be determined without reference to the property situated outside of the taxing country when that country is taxing on the basis of situs rather than domicile. This provision is common to the United States and United Kingdom agreements.
Article V provides for credits by the country of domicile in respect of duty paid to the other country on the same assets, thus eliminating double taxation.
Article VI provides for the period for refund of duty and claim for credit which is restricted to six years from date of death, as in the British agreement.
Article VII covers the exchange of information between the two governments.
Article VIII provides for bringing the agreement into force on the day of exchange of ratifications and relates it to estates of persons dying on or after that date, or before that date in the calendar year if the estate so elects.
Article IX provides for the agreement to remain in force for not less than three years, and for its renewal.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext:
On January 27 last, as reported on page 601 of Hansard, I made a preliminary announcement on the government's intention in regard to the continuation of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. I do not know that I can add anything about the principle of the bill we propose to introduce. Hon. members can refer to that statement for details of the government's intentions.
I should like to make a few remarks by way of background giving reasons why we are introducing this legislation at this time. The Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was inaugurated in 1948 for a period of three years to assist Canadian gold mine operators in meeting greatly increased costs of production. Unlike other primary mine products, there had been no compensating increase in the price of gold. This measure was designed primarily to assist the high-cost or marginal mines to continue in operation over a difficult period and to maintain their dependent communities. Because of the high cost of production of gold, in relation to a fixed price, the gold mines made strenuous efforts to increase their efficiency and to keep their costs at a minimum.
In this they have been very successful, but in spite of these efforts the upward trend of cost has continued. This trend has been aggravated by the appreciation in the value of the Canadian dollar which, so far as gold mines are concerned, means that they receive less for their product. The recent change in the exchange rate will be welcomed by the

industry, I am sure. When the act expired in 1950 it was renewed, and has been continued to the end of 1954.
In the formula as originally designed there were two parts. The first was the rate of assistance. The second factor was the part of production to which the rate of assistance applied. These two factors have, from time to time, been modified to meet current conditions.
It is an advantage to the gold mines, in order to allow adequate planning, that the extension should be for a longer term than one year. As the economic conditions which necessitated the passing of the act continue to exist, it is now proposed to extend the act for 1955 and 1956 on a somewhat reduced basis.
As indicated to this house, the proposal to extend the act is based on a new formula which still maintains the two main factors on a revised basis. Under the new formula the rate of assistance is two-thirds of the amount by which the average cost of producing an ounce of gold from the mine during the year exceeds $26.50 per ounce. But the rate paid per ounce will in no event exceed $12.33.	,
In the old formula the number of production ounces to which assistance applied was dependent on a base year which had been defined by the act. The new proposal does away with the base year. The rate of assistance will now apply to two-thirds of the total production of the current calendar year. This in effect simplifies the assistance calculations and maintains an equitable distribution of the payments to the mines receiving assistance.
It will be noted that the rate of assistance will not exceed $12.33 per ounce. This means in the application of the formula that the maximum allowable cost for the production of an ounce of gold under which payments will be made must not exceed $45.00. This is the same maximum allowable cost which was in effect in 1953 and 1954. In the new formula raising the factor in the rate of assistance from $18.00 to $26.50 makes some of the lower cost mines ineligible for assistance and distributes a proportionately greater part of the payments to the higher cost mines.
It is hoped that by this distribution of payments the higher cost mines will be able to continue and employment will be maintained. Payments under the act vary according to the cost in each mine of producing an ounce of gold. The new formula has been designed to aid the communities which are dependent on gold mines for their existence.

speechtext: In the discussion on the resolution we are dealing with the principle. I shall give those details later.

speechtext:
I am sure the committee will be glad to receive them. But I thought the minister's opening statement would have been a good place for him to give the house the benefit of a review of those operations on which statistical information is not yet available in report form.
One will wish, of course, to reserve until the bill has been made available some of the comments one might wish to make, but I am quite certain hon. members will approve the proposal to extend the life of the act. At the same time I think one must continue to express regret that it should be necessary for the government to bring forward this type of legislation.
Subsidy is no solution to the problem. Subsidy is not a satisfactory basis upon which to build the survival of any industry. It is not satisfactory so far as the taxpayer is concerned, and it is not a healthy condition for the industry itself. No matter what the formula may be, there are bound to be inequities in it and in its application. The minister is proposing tonight that there should be a revision of the formula to be applied. Well, this is going to mean, of course, that for some mines there will be substantially less assistance to be had under this act. Every time you introduce a subsidy, Mr. Chairman, and set forth the formula upon which it is to be applied, you create the necessity of drawing the line somewhere. There will be some inside and some outside it, and that cannot be regarded as a healthy state of affairs. Similarly every time the
1580	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act formula is changed some are hurt by the change, while it may be that some are helped by it.
This is not the kind of solution the industry has sought, but it is necessary as long as a proper solution is not forthcoming. Fundamentally, the reason there must be a subsidy until such time as the government brings forward an adequate solution is that the problem of the gold mines has been created largely by governments. I do not say by the Canadian government, although it has participated in the action of which I speak. But it is a problem created by governments in general. It is the problem of the fixed price for the product of the gold mining industry. And because the Canadian dollar first of all rose to par and then later to a premium in relation to the United States dollar, the value of the product, measured in terms of its price in the United States, instead of rising has actually been falling for some years. The governments have set the fixed price, and at the same time costs of production have been rising.
It is not too much to say, sir, that now, and for some years past, this important gold mining industry has been languishing. Many mines have been closed. The communities which have depended upon the gold mining industry have suffered in consequence. Development operations and the search for new mines, of course, were arrested years ago. No Canadian, in my submission, can contemplate what has happened to the gold mining industry without very serious misgivings.
There were days, and we would do well to remind ourselves of them, sir, when this country owed much to the gold mining industry, and when indeed that industry contributed as much as any other single factor to the survival of the Canadian economy, during the depression days. We always had a market for our product. It was a profitable market in those days; it is not a very profitable market today. We hope that depression days will never come back, but it would be a bold man or woman who would say that the day will not come when we shall need to rely upon the gold mining industry again to bring health and strength to the Canadian economy.
This measure is no solution. I can only describe it as I described it on a former occasion, as an artificial, temporary, stop-gap, hand-to-mouth palliative. It is necessary in order to assure the survival of some mines. It has not assured the survival of many of the mines that were in production when it came into effect. As a matter of fact, sir, if you will look at page 10 of the report on the administration of this act for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1954, you will see that from


a maximum of 122 in 1949 the number of mines which have been in receipt of aid under this act has shown a steady decline. In 1953 that number had been reduced to 70. What the figure is for 1954 I hope the minister will tell us; but whatever that figure may be it is quite evident that, in view of the revision of the formula, the number of mines which will receive assistance under this act in 1955 and 1956 will show a further reduction.
It may be that some of the mines which have been in receipt of aid, and which will not receive aid in 1955 and 1956, are not marginal mines and are not going to be compelled to abandon their operations. But, sir, that table on page 10 points a lesson which is worthy of the attention of all hon. members. The number of producing gold mines has shrunken in this period, and that shrinkage does pose serious questions and does create serious dangers, not simply for the communities that are dependent upon the gold mining industry but to a substantial degree for the whole Canadian economy.
The minister has stated that, with a view to giving assistance to the industry in looking ahead, it is now proposed that the subsidy aid scheme should be extended for two years. That, of course, is better than one. It at least lets those mines which are dependent upon this type of aid know that the aid will be available for another 22 months. But, sir, that is not enough. If the house approves this measure and the bill which is to follow, it cannot assume that it has discharged its responsibility for another two years. It is the duty of the government, it is the duty of the house, to be searching and searching resolutely for something much more satisfactory than a stop-gap measure of this kind.
What is required is a solution. It cannot be this measure. More is required than is to be found here. We have not heard from the government one word indicating what is its policy with reference to the search for a solution, or what its conception of the solution is. Is the government's conception of the proper solution an increase in the price of gold? I refer to the statement made by Mr. Abbott on April 13, 1953, when this measure was last under discussion in the house. At page 3797 of Hansard of that year, he said:
I have repeatedly stated In this house. Mr. Chairman, that the Canadian government, as the second largest gold producer in the world, would be delighted if the price of gold were increased.
Apparently the government, at least two years ago, approved of an increase in the price of gold. What is the government's position today? Does the government now, in

1955, still approve of an increase in the price of gold? That is my first question to the minister.
Second, if the government does approve of an increase in the price of gold, what is it doing to seek such an increase? We know that the increase in the price of gold must await decision or at least concurrence on the part of the United States government, because it is the greatest purchaser of gold in the world. It is the assured market for gold. Then what is the Canadian government doing, if it still believes there ought to be an increase in the price of gold, to urge upon the United States government that increase? I ask that question of the minister.
Again, from time to time, representations have been made to the government by the provincial ministers of mines in this regard. I ask the minister what position he has taken, what position the government here has taken in the face of representations coming from the department of mines of the provincial governments in this regard.
We are hearing much talk about the possibility of the restoration of convertibility of exchange. There have been intimations from different quarters that the return of convertibility may be closer than some had thought. Well, the return of convertibility is something we should all be seeking, all be hoping for, because of the substantial benefits that convertibility of exchange would contribute to the world's trading relations. It has special interest for Canada because of the extent to which we rely upon the market in the United Kingdom for the disposal of our large exportable surplus of food.
In the interests of convertibility, let us realize that gold is going to play, gold is bound to play, an important part in any plans that are made either by the sterling bloc or by the free world in general with a view to restoring either immediately or by stages, either on a partial basis or on a complete basis, convertibility of exchange. Then what is the government doing in the way of encouraging that restoration of convertibility and seeing that gold, in which this country is so much interested, plays its proper and important role in the restoration of convertibility?
Again, this matter being of such importance not only to Canada but to South Africa and to other parts of the commonwealth and empire, I ask, did the Prime Minister embrace the opportunity at the recent conference of prime ministers of the commonwealth to raise this question?
We have had only the most fragmentary and vague reports about what was done at that conference. Was no consideration given
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act to economic problems? Was no consideration given to this important matter of the restoration of convertibility? Together with South Africa, did Canada show its keen interest in seeking for gold, and for gold producers, recognition of their problems and a better price for their product, in developing policies within the commonwealth which will improve the position of the gold producing countries? When I say for the commonwealth I mean principally South Africa and Canada. Therefore I ask, what was done by the government at the prime ministers' conference in this regard? Was any attempt made by the Prime Minister representing Canada, a great gold producer, to seek concerted policies which will assist the gold producing countries of the commonwealth?
Finally, sir, let us all recognize that while the gold standard does not exist today, and while the place occupied by gold in relation to currencies may not be what it once was, nevertheless gold occupies a vital place in all the world's trading and exchange relations today.
It is an undeniable fact that all the countries of the world still want gold. That desire is not confined to the free world alone. Russia, itself a large gold producer, has apparently been seeking the means of increasing its supply of gold. Let us not think for one moment that gold has lost any of its value in the eyes of the nations. All the nations still place gold in a position of first importance as the medium of international exchange. The stability which has existed in our trading relations and in the exchange relations between countries owes more to gold than many people today realize.
Amid all the exchange fluctuations in the world today the fact that gold is still being sought by all countries and is still being bought by the United States at a fixed price, and the fact that that country is prepared to go on buying all the gold that is offered, has contributed much stability to the world. Indeed, in that respect gold has been the one stable reference point in the exchange relations of the countries of the world. Gold is still an important hedge for us as well as for other nations against depression. It is the basis of much of the confidence in trading relations which exist in the world. It is still the principal international standard and the principal international medium of exchange.
Let us then recognize its importance; and for Canada, as a leading gold producer in the world, let us realize its special importance as undergirding and strengthening the Canadian economy. While the present measure must be supported, let us not be content with temporary stop-gap policies of this kind, but

Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act let us see to it that we apply our best efforts and utmost intelligence to seeking a satisfactory long-term solution. I hope we will hear more about this policy from the government tonight.

May I say to the hon. members that this resolution is of concern to a large number of Canadians throughout the country. In addition, there are many farmers and settlers who are established on lands that would not be worth tilling today were it not for that industry. In addition, businessmen have invested their savings in firms that would have to close their doors should that industry come to a standstill. Moreover, a large number of Canadians, who are employed in numerous industries scattered throughout the country, are benefiting indirectly from gold mining operations. They are interested in this industry and they should be given consideration.
Of course, this resolution is of particular interest to the 130,000 Canadians living in cities, towns and mining centres, some 30 in number in Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba, British Columbia, Yukon and the Northwest Territories. Moreover, Mr. Chairman, I repeat that we should not forget that the livelihood of many farmers and settlers established on lands in the vicinity of mining centres in the provinces I have just mentioned, depends almost exclusively [DOT] on the gold mining industry. Those people are greatly concerned because the survival of this industry is of vital importance to them.
In the county of Villeneuve alone, which I have the honour to represent in this house, 15 gold mines are in operation. I must say, Mr. Chairman, that our people were very happy to learn that this legislation was to be extended for a further two-year period. In fact, the 160,000 people in northwestern Quebec were confident that the government would extend this Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. They were not disappointed and are thankful to the government for all that has been done to help the development of our natural resources and the progress of our mining districts.


I have received a number of letters and resolutions from municipal councils, school boards or chambers of commerce of my constituency. Copies of these documents have been forwarded to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) and the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham). All those requests take national interest into account and deal with the problem in an objective way.
In order that the importance of this industry to those whose livelihood is directly dependent upon it can be readily understood, I could hardly do better than to quote certain passages from a resolution sent to me by the town council of Malartic.
Here, Mr. Chairman, we have a town of 7,000 people, with highly efficient municipal services, and where schools have a capacity of 2,000 pupils. Now the only industry here is that of gold mining.
Here are the words used by the members of the town council:
The gold mining industry has played a very important part in the history of this country; it has contributed and continues to contribute to a very large extent to the development of our natural resources.
For the past six years the industry has suffered a great deal from the fact that the price of its product has been maintained at pre-war levels and the situation, far from improving, seems to be getting worse.
The gold mining industry provides permanent employment for more than 20,000 people who are directly employed by it. Moreover it provides work for a large number of other Canadians in agriculture, the lumber trade or manufacturing. If too many gold mines were forced to suspend operations, through lack of adequate revenue, this would materially contribute to an increase in unemployment.
The assistance given under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act to that industry has been of material help in enabling many mines to stay in operation. Without it, several would be forced to close down.
At the end of its petition, the municipal council of Malartic expresses the following wish:
We ask that this act be extended for at least one more year.
Representatives of the municipal councils, the school boards, and the chambers of commerce of the other municipalities in my riding have expressed similar views, and all concur in the belief that the closing down of our gold mines would create a great deal of unemployment.
Mr. Chairman, those letters, those resolutions to which I have directed your attention, speak for themselves. They are clear and to the point. They make us grasp the national

importance of the industry and, in addition, they prove that the gold mining industry is a source of steady employment and that, therefore, it must be kept in a healthy condition. They represent the views of experienced businessmen, who know what they want, who are interested above all in the welfare of the communities whose business they manage, and who are anxious to plead the case of all those who live in mining communities across Canada. Their arguments can hardly be gainsaid and I ask the committee to take them into consideration.
I wish to congratulate the minister for giving the house in advance, on January 27 last, the amendments which the government intended to introduce to the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. It was very important for the industry and all those interested in it to know as soon as possible what the outlook was.
As far as 1 am concerned, I was happy to know that the benefits of the new act were to apply to the production of the years 1955 and 1956. On the other hand, I am somewhat disappointed to see that those benefits will be reduced, perhaps a little too much in some cases.
On the basis of the new formula, it is obvious that the average rate of assistance, per ounce, will be greatly reduced. Mines for which production costs per ounce amount to $26.50 or less will be completely excluded. On the other hand, those for which production costs per ounce come to $40 or more will get greater assistance.
However, we are sorry to see that several gold mines, whose production costs per ounce are between $30 and $35, are due for a considerable reduction of their net income, which is already low. The operators of a good number of these mines would like to be in a position to pay still higher salaries to their employees, and they are anxious to speed up their exploration work in order to improve the situation and thus reduce costs of production, but I doubt very much that in such circumstances they will find it possible to do so.
We should not forget, Mr. Chairman, that the situation of the gold mines, instead of improving in the course of last year, has deteriorated.
Since the industry is subject to the rising value of the Canadian dollar in comparison with the United States dollar, the price paid by the mint for gold has constantly decreased. For a full realization of the prejudice suffered by the gold mines, one only has to know that the price paid for an ounce of gold during the years 1952, 1953 and 1954 was

At this stage I merely want to point out that the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act is an extremely important act in our general economy. I am in complete agreement with the hon. member for Eglinton that the payment of these subsidies is only a temporary stopgap, and is by no means a solution to the problem with which the gold mining industry confronts us in this country. In the introduction to the report on the administration of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act for the year ended March 31, 1952, we were told that the act was designed primarily to assist the high-cost or marginal mines to continue in operation over a difficult period and to maintain their dependent communities.
What has become evident over the years, of course, is that the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act has been subsidizing other than marginal mines. Since the inception of this act the bulk of our subsidies has gone to mines that cannot, by any stretch of the

That period of difficulty is still with us, and there is little prospect that the end of the gold mining industry's difficulties is yet in sight. Helpful as the subsidies are to the gold mining industry and to some extent, I suppose, to the communities concerned with gold mining, they certainly are not the answer to the problems with which we are confronted in the matter of gold mining. More far-reaching measures than providing for the payment of annual subsidies are needed to solve those problems.
I am not sure that an increase in the price of gold, as the hon. member for Eglinton suggested, would be the answer to those problems at all. When the price of gold was raised in the 1930's from $20.67 an ounce, I think it was, to $35 an ounce, the social problems connected with the gold mining industry continued. About all that happened when the price of gold was raised was that instead of being satisfied with ore which yielded one-third of an ounce of gold for every ton, we proceeded to mill ore from which we could extract as little as one-quarter of an ounce per ton. That was the one big advance brought about by the rise in the price of gold in the thirties. If tomorrow the price of gold were raised to $50 or $60 an ounce, what would most likely happen is that we would proceed to mine and mill still lower grades of ore, ore that would possibly give us much less than a quarter of an ounce of gold per ton.
There is no assurance whatever that the social problems connected with gold mining would be solved by a simple rise in the price of gold. As I indicated, much more far-reaching measures are needed to correct the social ills of the gold mining industry, and when the bill is before us I shall take advantage of that opportunity to discuss what in my opinion are some of these far-reaching measures.
