Mr. Chairman, members representing constituencies in which important gold mining operations are carried on hoped that the government's cost-aid program would be continued at least without reduction, and I am no exception. But the government with its special information and with all the evidence before it felt bound to bring in a somewhat modified version of emergency assistance.
As far as gold mining operations in the Yukon are concerned, the picture is a mixed one. The new formula continues federal assistance to the industry on the basis of giving a greater measure of help to the mines


which need help the most. In other words when a mine's cost of operating is low, assistance will be on a reduced scale. In the case of high-cost mines, in order to keep as many of them as possible in operation the aid given under E.G.M.A. will be relatively higher.
Possibly the most important feature of the proposed new bill is the extension of the cost aid over the period of the next two years. Making the policy apply over two years instead of one will enable the gold mines to plan their operations with greater assurance. The two-year provision carries into effect an important recommendation in the brief submitted last fall to the federal government by the Canadian Metal Mining Association.
I believe it would serve a useful purpose, Mr. Chairman, to consider briefly the history and intention of this cost-aid legislation. First of all, what was the basic reason for introducing E.G.M.A. in 1948? It was not designed as a cure for all the ills of the industry. It was not intended particularly as a method of increasing production. Rather it was planned, as I understand it, to provide emergency help over a difficult and, it was hoped, limited period of time. However, the conditions that compelled the introduction of E.G.M.A. have persisted since 1948. Some Canadians have the mistaken idea that because most nations have dropped the gold standard, gold is no longer a useful metal. Actually when the nations adopted the device of managed instead of gold-based currencies, gold became more than ever a servant of man rather than his master.
The value of most managed currencies is still expressed in terms of gold content. The real strength of gold is in its universal acceptance as an international means of payment. It is in effect a lubricant which helps to keep the mechanism of international trade functioning smoothly. For example, Canada maintains reserves in the form of gold to meet obligations that may arise from time to time in our foreign trade accounts. If we buy more from any country than we sell to that country, then settlement or adjustment is arranged in gold.
But I regard the gold mining industry as essential to Canadian progress and prosperity for other reasons as well. A healthy gold mining industry in this country means a healthy mining industry generally and a stronger, richer Canada. The industry provides employment as well as important markets for machinery and supplies. More than that, gold mining is the mainspring of the entire mining economy, especially in the north. It is the pioneer industry of the north, and much of Canada's future growth is bound up in northern development.

The search for gold seems to spur the search for other minerals as well. Directly and indirectly the gold mining industry has contributed much to the solid growth of the entire nation. I sincerely hope that, even with the modification proposed, cost aid will enable gold mining operations to be carried on, thus sustaining the northern communities which its operations have been mainly instrumental in founding and which still depend on the industry for their survival. The recent devaluation of the Canadian dollar in terms of the United States dollar will provide a substantial benefit to our gold mining operations which will offset in some degree the reduction in gold mining assistance.
Lest we forget the contribution of the Klondike to Canada's progress and prosperity, I want to again remind the house that it was gold from the Klondike at the turn of the century that started Canada on her twentieth century era of advance and development. I am confident, Mr. Chairman, that the minister is keenly interested in proposals to promote Canada's mineral development generally, and I hope more especially in those fields which may be effective in encouraging greater gold and other mining activity in the northern territories.

The hon. member for Eglinton has referred to the fact that the purchase of gold by the United States government has had a stabilizing influence on the industry. There is no doubt about that. True, the price probably is not as high as the Canadian industry needs; nevertheless, were it not for the fact that the United States is willing to purchase gold there is no doubt the industry would be much worse off than it is today.
Questions have been asked as to what the government has done to influence the United States to raise the price of gold. I have not been present at international conferences, but I do know the matter has been discussed frankly with the United States government. On one occasion I had the privilege of talking to the President of the United States and asking him very pertinent questions in this connection. He cited many arguments pro and con, and ended his remarks by saying, "My advice to you is, don't make any mistakes in a hurry." I do not know what one can take from that remark; but I can assure you if we thought the United States was going to raise the price of gold by several dollars within the next few months we would not have introduced emergency gold mining assistance for a two-year period.

I do not know what other questions my hon. friend would like to have answered. I made a few notes as he was speaking. I agree that the gold mining industry is a stabilizing influence in a time of depression, and makes a great contribution to the development of our country. Until recent years it was the main incentive to take prospectors and developers into the wilderness to help roll back the frontier northward, to give our country depth as well as breadth.
In recent years other minerals perhaps more spectacular-and I am thinking particularly of uranium-have been replacing gold as the main incentive. But gold is still important. It is a commodity that has a ready market, so long as the United States is prepared to buy it. We do not have to send salesmen abroad to sell it. Gold has great value in maintaining our exchange balance with the United States and other countries. The gold mining industry employs between 18,000 and 19,000 people. It is a great consumer of raw products, products of the farm, products of our steel industry and of our forests. Many communities are entirely dependent upon gold mines. These people are producing a valuable product for Canada, the sale of which provides funds to buy from other countries goods required by Canadians. We believe the gold mining industry should be maintained, and that is why we are introducing this emergency gold mining assistance measure. We are hopeful that a permanent solution will develop.
The industry has done a great deal to help itself. They have reduced their operating costs and are increasing the production of gold per man day. I believe they are doing everything possible to put their own industry in order, and that is one good reason why they deserve further assistance. The amount we propose to pay in the next two years is considerably less than what the 1954 payments will be.
Under the proposal no mine with costs below $26.50 will receive assistance. I do not think many hon. members would argue that they should. Previously the number of ounces to which the rate of assistance applied was dependent upon a base year, which the mine had the privilege of choosing. Now the base year has been abolished and payment will be made on a basis of two-thirds of current production. We think that is a fair way of applying the assistance.
Some of the mining associations and several individual mines have been in communication with us since the announcement was made, and they believe the proposal we are now putting forward is a fair one, although some of them have expressed the wish that there was a little more money in it.

Therefore the industry as a whole, although there may be fewer mines, did increase its production. We do not think this new formula will discourage production. We do not think any mines will close because of this revised formula. If they close it will be because of lack of ore, or for other reasons.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext:
I do not think a great deal can usefully be added at this stage, except to point out that although the minister may be correct in saying that this formula will not result in the closing of any mines-I think 50433-101
that is questionable-certainly it will result in the reduction of assistance to efficient mines. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra was certainly right when he says that it penalizes efficiency. I have an idea of what it is estimated this will mean in the reduction of assistance to the Bralorne mine, and it is a very substantial sum.
The minister might say that the production of gold increased last year. Certainly, however, if the assistance is going to be reduced as drastically as is indicated by the figures I have it is going to bring about the result that the most efficient operator is going to have to go after his high grade ore and leave the low grade ore. I am informed that this will result in a situation where the low grade ore will be sealed off, and it will be virtually impossible and certainly uneconomic to go back after it when they finish extracting the high grade ore in that area. The reasons for that are really self-evident.
The effects of this proposed legislation cannot be simply written off by saying that it is not going to close any gold mines. It is going to reduce the assistance, particularly to the efficient operators. I cannot believe that this will have anything but a damaging effect upon their whole operation. I do not see how it can have any other effect than to reduce the wages and the standard of living of the miners generally, which is equally as important as the consideration that it will reduce the over-all efficiency of the mining operations from the point of view of making the best use and the widest possible extraction of all grades of ore in their mines.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: I have one question.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext: I should like to get some comment from the minister on the statement which has been made to me that this will result in the virtual closing off of the lower grade of ore in the mines.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO 1955 AND 1956
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman, I do not believe that at all. One of the most efficient mines, in my opinion, has the lowest grade of ore. I believe that all mines are operating efficiently regardless of whether or not they have been fortunate enough to find a high grade ore deposit. The particular mine to which I refer has been operating on a very low grade of ore, and will receive more assistance under this proposal. The mines which are now operating in a good ore body will receive correspondingly less assistance. I do not believe this will result in inefficiency or highgrading. It may be of interest to hon. members to know that over the 10-year period 1942 to 1952 the maximum variation among all mines in the grade of ore has been only two-one hundredths of an ounce per ton.

Historic Sites and Monuments Act There is no reason to believe that the reduction to about the 1953 level of payments will result in highgrading or inefficiency.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Lesage (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, TRAVELLING EXPENSES, ETC.
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 182, to amend the Historic Sites and Monuments Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, TRAVELLING EXPENSES, ETC.
speechtext: Has the minister a short statement to make?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, TRAVELLING EXPENSES, ETC.
speechtext: There is not much I could add to the explanatory note at the top of the bill which has been distributed. I thought I would not intervene in the debate now, but would wait until the conclusion of the debate when hon. members had raised their questions.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, TRAVELLING EXPENSES, ETC.
speechtext:
I have a few brief comments which I would like to make at this stage. I take it that the objective of this bill is to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the historic sites and monuments board, and I heartily support any legislation which is calculated to attain that end. I am pleased, too, to see that the scope and definition of "historic site" have been widened to include buildings or structures that are of national interest by reason of age or architectural design.
I think it would be well for this house at this time to pay tribute to the excellent work which has been done, chiefly on a voluntary basis, by the members of the historic sites and monuments board over the years. They have rescued for us as a nation and almost against our will some of the great historic treasures and physical reminders of our historic past, which we now hold in trust and which we should be prepared to hand on to posterity.


We as a nation in the past have been woefully negligent in taking a proper interest in the physical things which are associated with the historic and the heroic deeds of our ancestors. I think I could not do better than quote one of our better known statesmen of the past in this connection. Joseph Howe once said:
A wise nation preserves its records, gathers up its muniments, decorates the tombs of its illustrious dead, repairs its great structures, and fosters national pride and love of country, by perpetual references to the sacrifices and glories of the past.
I think that is advice which is still completely applicable to the present time. When considering Canadian history generally there is a tendency, which may be caused by the history textbooks which are used in some of the provinces, to think that Canadian history is entirely embraced in a recording of the events which took place in the St. Lawrence valley and in what now are the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. We should realize that in recording our history and in marking places which are connected with our early history we should have in mind the total history of what is now Canada.
I would like to quote briefly from an article which appeared in the Halifax Chronicle on January 1, 1924. It was written by Dr. J. Clarence Webster, who at that time was a member of the historic sites and monuments board of Canada. He says:
While in the United States recently, I took the opportunity of visiting the region, which for centuries has been the chief thoroughfare between old Canada and the American colonies, lake Champlain being its central feature. No area of North America is richer in historic traditions, except, possibly, Nova Scotia or Quebec.
I point that out in order to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, that on the east coast we have an area that is steeped in history, connected as it is with the early history of exploration and with the economic adventures connected with the fisheries and the fur trade on the Atlantic coast.
I note that this bill proposes to add two members to the board. In general I think it is an excellent thing that the board should be strengthened. I note that the increase is to be made by appointing an extra member for each of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. That is probably a very good thing. By way of explanation the bill says:
Because of the large volume of work arising from the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, it is considered necessary to have two representatives from each of these provinces on the board.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, TRAVELLING EXPENSES, ETC.
speechtext: It was recommended by the Massey commission.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, TRAVELLING EXPENSES, ETC.
speechtext:
I recognize that fact. I see that right here in the Massey commission

report. But immediately after that, at page 348, I also see this:
Two members to be nominated by the council of the Canadian Historical Association, similarly for five-year terms and similarly eligible for reappointment for one further term.
If only one of those two recommendations were to be complied with I would think it might be more advantageous at this time to appoint two members at large, so that outstanding historians from any part of Canada could be appointed as additional members to the board. In that connection, may I point out that the Massey commission also has this to say-and I agree with it most heartily- on the subject of work which should be done by the board in the near future. This is by way of work to be done by the board:
. . . giving special attention to the province of Newfoundland as singularly rich in records of the past;
The opinion of the Massey commission seems to be that Newfoundland is the area where the most work has to be done at the moment. I note also that Canada has a number of historic parks. As a matter of fact I believe that six of our ten provinces have them. I just mention this in passing. I am pleased to see that at the resolution stage the minister stated that action is to be taken to provide an historic park in Newfoundland.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, TRAVELLING EXPENSES, ETC.
speechtext: A national park.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, TRAVELLING EXPENSES, ETC.
speechtext: A national park? Not an historic park?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, TRAVELLING EXPENSES, ETC.
speechtext: No, not an historic park.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, TRAVELLING EXPENSES, ETC.
speechtext: I will introduce at this session legislation to provide for the establishment of a national park.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, TRAVELLING EXPENSES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am sorry I misread the minister's statement, but that only adds more force to my contention that action should be taken in the near future to create historic parks in the four provinces that do not have them. They are British Columbia, Alberta, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, I believe, if I am up to date.
I think it is important, too, that when historic events are commemorated it should be done in as artistic a way as possible. The work that has been done in the past by putting up markers is worth while, but I think perhaps some of those markers themselves could have more artistic value. In most cases they are just stone monuments. In Europe one sees pleasing artistic monuments. One that comes to my mind now is the French monument at the site of the battle of Waterloo, which shows the wounded French eagle. That is a monument that has some added significance.
Historic Sites and Monuments Act
I think it is vitally important that our young people growing up, especially, by means of the marking of historic sites and the preserving of historic buildings should have accurate knowledge of our history. I do not think it is good enough for our Canadian young people to get their history by extremely inaccurate United States-produced films of what is purported to be Canadian history. One that comes to my mind in the form of a film that was shown widely last year on what was supposed to be the early history of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police was called "Saskatchewan", I believe.
In that connection, we should not be misled by such fanciful literary efforts as the poem Evangeline. That may be a fine piece of literary work but, from a historical point of view, it is utter nonsense. It could not be further from the facts. I think our Canadian children should be made to realize that fact.
I also think it is important that, when historic places have been marked, anniversaries in connection with them be publicized in some way in order to refresh the minds, especially of young people, as to the historic significance of those areas. In that connection two anniversaries come to my mind immediately. As I have mentioned before, my home city of Charlottetown is this year celebrating its 100th anniversary of incorporation as a city. I notice that this year 1955 is another anniversary. It is the 200th anniversary of the establishment of the first post office in Canada. That post office was established in Halifax in 1755. The site is marked with a plaque which was put up by the historic sites and monuments board on Hollis street post office in Halifax.
Having said that, I want to say that I support this bill most heartily with the reservation I have pointed out, namely that I would prefer to see the two additional members of the board appointed as members at large rather than arbitrarily appointed from two of the provinces.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, TRAVELLING EXPENSES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to the house leader for arranging for the second reading of this bill to be called today. It seems to be a year as well as a day of anniversaries. The hon. member who has just taken his seat has referred to two important anniversaries. As hon. members are aware from a little question that I managed to get in on the orders of the day today, there is another anniversary that I have in mind. This is the 28th of February, 1955. Exactly 100 years ago today, on the 28th of February, 1855, the first post office in western Canada was opened. That post office was established in a private residence which was known as the

Historic Sites and Monuments Act Ross house, and it is still known by that name today. In 1855 the area now known as Winnipeg was, of course, what was called the Red River settlement; but even so, it had had an organized government for about 20 years, a local government having been formed under the authority of the council of Assini-boia back in 1835.
The Manitoba historical society has done a good deal of research into this matter and has found that the first sheriff, teacher and historian of the Red River settlement was Alexander Ross. It was his son William Ross who in February of 1855 was appointed postmaster by what was then known as the council of Assiniboia. In earlier days that council was appointed by Lord Selkirk. By 1855 it was under the Hudson's Bay Company. That was the situation when, a century ago today, William Ross began business as the first postmaster in western Canada. His house was a building constructed of squared logs which was situated on the banks of the Red river at the foot of what later became known as Market street, in what is now the constituency of Winnipeg North Centre. In more recent times the building has been moved to another location.
It is an historic site, Mr. Speaker, and the bill now before us proposes to extend the definition of an historic place to include buildings or structures that are of national interest by reason of age or architectural design, so Your Honour will recognize that I could not be more in order. The building has been moved to William Whyte park directly across the street from the Canadian Pacific Railway station in Winnipeg. I invite members who go through Winnipeg on the Canadian Pacific to use the time they have for a stopover there to go across the street and visit this very historic site.
It has been furnished in the style of the period, and this has been done through the efforts of the Manitoba historical society. On their behalf I also want to thank the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) for having arranged for a special cachet so that letters can still be posted from'Ross house bearing a stamp indicating that they were mailed in the first post office in western Canada.
We of the west, Mr. Speaker, have not yet formed the habit of spending much time in looking back, but once in a while on occasions such as this we do so briefly so that we may measure our progress and look forward to still greater achievements in the years that lie ahead. I hope this very important historic site will be recognized as such by the historic sites and monuments board, and I am very glad that this opportunity has arisen to draw attention to the


fact that this very day is the 100th anniversary of the opening of the first post office in western Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to support this measure. My remarks are going to be very brief because I was most anxious that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre should have the opportunity to tell the house of the anniversary of this first western post office in Winnipeg. I am not going to say anything further because I am prepared to forgo the remarks I intended to make at this time, for the sake of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, until we come to the estimates.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to take a few moments to note one fact. The minister now in charge of the department may not know of, and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) may not recall, an incident of two years ago when we were discussing the bill which established the historic sites and monuments board. I drew attention then to the fact that there was no need to appoint as a member of that board the curator of the national museum, not because of the person involved but because of the nature of his work which I thought was heavy enough without inflicting on him duties connected with this particular organization. I pointed out that the Massey commission had not recommended his appointment. I see by the bill that he has now been dropped by the board.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, TRAVELLING EXPENSES, ETC.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, TRAVELLING EXPENSES, ETC.
speechtext:
He is not named in the bill that we have before us. He may be named as an appointee of the minister, but if the minister has that thought in mind I would draw his attention to the remarks I made in that regard in the session of 1952-53, as found at page 1444 of Hansard, and the reasons I gave there.
The second point I should like to make is one to which the hon. member for Queens

drew attention, namely that the Massey commission recommended that two members of the board should be nominated by the council of the Canadian Historical Association. I advanced arguments in favour of that proposition on that occasion. Two years ago the minister had his opportunity to implement in full the recommendations of the Massey commission with regard to this board. He overlooked that opportunity and has simply enlarged the board by adding an additional member from Ontario and Quebec as recommended by the Massey commission. There are good reasons for following the other suggestion of permitting the council of the historical association to nominate

members to the board. I merely want to draw those comments to the attention of the minister, and perhaps in the course of another two years they may be acted upon.
